10.17586/2687-0568-2026-8-3-159-175.abstract: Ammonia is essential for fertilizers, chemicals, and emerging carbon-free energy systems, yet its conventional production relies on an energy-intensive process with substantial carbon dioxide emissions. Photoelectrocatalytic nitrogen reduction has emerged as a promising route for sustainable ammonia synthesis under mild conditions, combining solar light absorption with an electrochemical bias to activate the inert nitrogen molecule. This review examines recent progress in this field, focusing on the design of stable titanium dioxide-based photoanodes and selective photocathodes incorporating copper oxide and two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides such as molybdenum disulfide and tungsten disulfide. Synthesis strategies, fabrication methods, cell configurations, reaction mechanisms, and performance parameters are discussed. Key challenges, including the high activation barrier of nitrogen, competing hydrogen evolution, and nitrogen mass-transfer limitations, are analyzed alongside verification protocols and future directions for efficient, carbon-free ammonia production.

10.2139/ssrn.6168132.abstract: A series of alkaline-earth metal silicates AeSiO3 (Ae=Mg, Ca, Sr and Ba) were prepared and used as support for Ru-based catalysts for NH3 decomposition to COx-free hydrogen. Among them, Ru/CaSiO3 was found to be the best catalyst for this reaction, giving the NH3 conversion of 50.6 % and H2 generation rate of 16.94 mmol·g-1cat·min-1 at a gas hourly space velocity of 30,000 mL·g-1cat·h-1 and a reaction temperature of 450 oC, which increased by 203 %, 51 % and 64 % compared with those of Ru/MgSiO3, Ru/SrSiO3, and Ru/BaSiO3. Analysis of the structure-activity relationship revealed that the uniform dispersion of ruthenium nanoparticles over CaSiO3 support was attributed to the large specific surface area of CaSiO3. Therefore, the number of active sites and basic sites has significantly increased. The strong basicity of the support provided ruthenium nanoparticles with high electron density, resulting in the high activity of Ru/CaSiO3 for NH3 decomposition.

10.2139/ssrn.6205774.abstract: Molybdenum disulfide quantum dots (MoS2 QDs) are recognized as noteworthy antibacterial nanomaterials owing to their inherent peroxidase-like properties. In this study, we successfully enhanced the synthesis of ammonia by Klebsiella pasteurii Sb-24 using MoS2 QDs and elucidated the underlying mechanism. Our investigation revealed that the synthesized MoS2 QDs exhibit superoxide dismutase/peroxidase-like activities and when incorporated into K. pasteurii Sb-24, they effectively mitigate intracellular levels of reactive oxygen species. Moreover, the MoS2 QDs nanozymes accelerated the logarithmic growth phase of Klebsiella cells, improved cellular permeability, and enhanced nitrogen fixation activity. Through optimization, the biohybrid system achieved a peak NH4+ production of 0.42±0.01 μg·mL-1, surpassing untreated cells by over 3.2 times. Further investigations unveiled that MoS2 QDs nanozymes induced modifications in the functional groups of cellular proteins and facilitated electron transfer into Klebsiella cells efficiently. These outcomes were supported by the upregulation of genes (particularly nifD, nifH, nifK and nifA) associated with nitrogen fixation. This study introduces an effective approach for boosting ammonia production using MoS2 QDs nanozymes and establishes a sturdy foundation for future research on biomanufacturing employing hybrid systems.

10.2139/ssrn.6221998.abstract: Anaerobic digestate is rich in nitrogen, and its treatment poses substantial challenges to conventional processes due to its ammonium concentration, high alkalinity, and low biodegradable carbon content. In this study, microbial fuel cells (MFCs) were investigated for the treatment of digestate. An orthogonal experimental design was employed to evaluate the effects of influent ammonium concentration (100–300 mg/L), pH (8–10), and external resistance (100–1000 Ω) on nitrogen removal and electricity generation. The MFC consistently achieved high nitrate removal efficiencies (>97%), whereas ammonium removal was strongly condition-dependent. The highest ammonium removal efficiency (66.6%) and total nitrogen removal efficiency (84.8%) were obtained at 300 mg/L NH4+, pH 10, and an external resistance of 1000 Ω. Although pH was identified as the dominant factor influencing performance, microbial community analysis revealed the enrichment of Paracoccus and Thauera, suggesting that nitrogen removal was mainly governed by the coupling of heterotrophic nitrification–aerobic denitrification with bioelectrochemical processes. This work demonstrates the feasibility of using MFCs for the treatment of high-strength digestate and provides valuable insights into the optimization of nitrogen-rich wastewater management.

10.2139/ssrn.6276819.abstract: The electrochemical properties of hard carbon (HC) anode largely depend on synthesis protocol. We performed a comparative study of coconut-shell-derived HC anode materials prepared using the flash Joule heating and the heat treatment methods. It is found that Joule heating offers HC materials with a wider interlayer spacing of graphite crystallites, a higher closed pore volume and richer surface chemistry compared with heat treatment. An HC sample prepared at 1500 °C using the Joule heating method delivers a Na+ storage capacity of 294 mAh g-1 at 0.2C with 89% capacity retention after 400 cycles. However, the initial Coulombic efficiency of the HC anode prepared using the Joule heating method is lower than that of the heat-treated counterpart anode, primarily due to more surface defective sites of the former than the latter. A full cell fabricated with the HC sample prepared using the Joule heating method as anode and a commercial sodium vanadium phosphate as cathode delivers an energy density of 162 Wh kg-1 at 0.2C with 87% capacity retained after 300 cycles. This work highlights the pros and cons of flash Joule heating in processing coconut-derived HC anode materials for Na+ batteries.

10.2139/ssrn.6294974.abstract: Green ammonia synthesis using renewable energy, featuring zero-carbon emissions, is crucial for replacing the conventional Haber-Bosch process. Recent studies have highlighted the great potential of plasma-electrocatalysis cascade strategies for this purpose. To advance such systems toward practical implementation, we developed an integrated reactor that enables simultaneous plasma oxidation and electrocatalytic NOx− reduction, achieving continuous ammonia synthesis directly from air and water. In this system, a gliding arc discharge employed to oxidize N2 was optimized and diagnosed, delivering a low specific energy consumption (SEC) of 3.05 kW h mol−1. Meanwhile, a Co3O4/CuO electrocatalyst was developed, achieving an NH3 yield rate of 0.84 mmol h−1 cm−2 with a Faradaic efficiency of 92.1%. More importantly, the integrated reactor demonstrates a pronounced synergistic effect: the plasma not only continuously supplies NOx− but also generates short-lived reactive species that actively promote the subsequent electrocatalytic reduction. Consequently, the cascade system achieves a NH3 yield rate of 8.93 mmol h−1 with an overall SEC of 4.06 kW h mol−1 from N2 to NH3. This work demonstrates the unique advantages of integrated reactor coupling plasma and electrocatalysis, offering a promising pathway toward sustainable ammonia production.

10.2139/ssrn.6314738.abstract: The energy-inefficient and environmentally unsustainable nature of conventional ammonia synthesis necessitates alternative nitrogen fixation pathways powered by renewable electricity. Herein, we develop a coupled in-water plasma-electrochemical strategy for sustainable ammonia production, in which dinitrogen is first activated by in-water plasma to generate a dilute NOx- solution, followed by electrochemical reduction to ammonia. Enabled by a nano-Cu4O3 electrocatalyst, ammonia is produced from low-concentration NOx- at a rate of 5.58 mg mgcat-1 h-1 at -0.47 V vs. RHE. Mechanistic investigations attribute the superior activity to in situ formed Cu-Cu4O3 interfacial sites, which markedly reduce the energy barriers for proton-coupled electron transfer. As a result of the plasma-electrochemical synergy, the system achieves an electrical-to-chemical energy conversion efficiency of 14.8%. And the energy consumption of this system attains 4.63 MJ mol-1 with air as the nitrogen source. These performance metrics position this work among the state-of-the-art electrically powered nitrogen-to-ammonia technologies, offering a carbon-neutral and energy-sustainable paradigm for ammonia synthesis.

10.2139/ssrn.6366865.abstract: Simultaneous ammonia production as a heat-releasing process and cyclohexane and methanol dehydrogenation as endothermic reactions are simulated for the first time in a thermally coupled system. Thermal coupling of these reactions enables us to use the heat generated by the exothermic process instead of relying on heat-supplying equipment. Consequently, the suggested design is expected to yield a substantial decrease in energy usage and prevent the generation of associated pollutants typically produced in conventional furnace-based systems. Besides, no hydrogen is required for ammonia production, as dehydrogenation processes in the same reactor entirely supply the hydrogen needed. The present research utilizes a one-dimensional mathematical model for steady-state operation, assuming that the feed streams flow axially through homogeneous catalyst beds with non-constant physical characteristics. Eventually, results indicate improvements in methanol and cyclohexane conversions from 0.476 to 0.498 and from 0.844 to 0.875, respectively, while nitrogen conversion decreases slightly.

10.2139/ssrn.6386949.abstract: Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction (eNO3RR) offers a sustainable, carbon-neutral route to ammonia (NH3) synthesis. However, its practical deployment is severely hampered by the kinetic mismatch between nitrate deoxygenation and intermediate hydrogenation, exacerbated by competing hydrogen evolution (HER). Here, we report a heterometallic interfacial engineering strategy to synchronize these tandem kinetics using a dynamically reconstructed Ni/Cu oxide nanoarray (h-Ni-Cu1-2O/CF). Comprehensive in situ spectroscopy and theoretical simulations reveal that the precatalyst undergoes structural reconstruction to in situ exsolve metallic Ni nanodomains anchored by highly stable Ni-O-Cu coordination motifs under working conditions. This unique bifunctional interface fundamentally stabilizes active Cuδ+ sites for accelerated initial deoxygenation, while the electronically modulated Ni sites act as an optimal ”hydrogen pump”. This configuration efficiently channels active hydrogen (*H) to the nitrogenous intermediates, eradicating the NO2- hydrogenation bottleneck and silencing the HER. Consequently, the catalyst achieves a near-unity Faradaic efficiency of 98.6% and sustains unprecedented performance at an aggressive industrial-level current density of 3000 mA cm-2 (NH3 production rate: 12.1 mmol h-1 cm-2). Furthermore, integrated into a continuous-flow system, macroscopic quantities (>5 g) of high-purity solid (NH4)2SO4 were successfully recovered. This work establishes a versatile interfacial design principle for coordinating proton-coupled multi-electron tandem electrocatalysis.

10.2139/ssrn.6429501.abstract: The nitrate reduction reaction involves the transfer of eight electrons and the participation of nine protons, generating multiple intermediates with rich spin characteristics, thereby introducing complexity into the development of catalytic materials. In this study, MXene-supported mesoporous carbon structures are synthesized to anchor cobalt nanoparticles (MXene@MC-Co), with the aim of regulating the spin polarization intensity of the cobalt nanoparticles to balance the interactions between key adsorbed species and the catalyst. Combined theoretical and experimental analyses reveal that the MXene@MC support can effectively reduce the spin polarization degree of cobalt nanoparticles, thereby promoting efficient hydrogenation and ammonia synthesis. The MXene@MC-Co catalyst exhibits excellent electrocatalytic performance toward nitrate reduction, delivering an ammonia yield of 5500 μg h-1 mgcat.-1 with a Faradaic efficiency of 80.12%. The Zn-NO3- battery assembled with this catalyst achieves an outstanding power density of 8 mW cm-2 and a Faradaic efficiency of 87.4% at a current density of 12 mA cm-2, enabling the simultaneous synthesis of ammonia and electrical energy output. This work not only demonstrates the feasibility of regulating metal spin polarization behavior via support engineering but also reveals the crucial role of spin polarization in driving efficient nitrate reduction.

10.2139/ssrn.6443467.abstract: Heterogeneous metal-catalyzed tandem ammonia borane (AB) dehydrogenation and nitroarene hydrogenation is a powerful strategy for valuable aniline production. However, common heterogeneous catalysts are powder materials, requiring high-speed centrifugation or vacuum filtration for post-reaction separation. Herein, copper oxide nanowires in situ grown on nickel foam (CuxO NWs/NF) were facilely prepared as a self-standing catalyst for nitroarene hydrogenation with AB. This 3D magnetic foam-supported catalyst exhibits excellent recyclability, separability, and selectivity, tolerating various functional groups and affording target aminoarenes in good to excellent yields. Benefiting from its large size and the ferromagnetism of NF, it can be easily separated using tweezers or a magnet. Notably, CuxO (true active sites) was unexpectedly doped with boron from AB during the reaction. After the reaction, metallic copper was identified as the dominant component of the catalyst. Reaction mechanism studies show nitroarene reduction proceeds via a condensation pathway as azobenzene and azoxybenzene intermediates were captured. This work provides a proof-of-concept for nanocatalyst immobilization and paves the way for applying self-supporting electrocatalysts in organic transformations.

10.2139/ssrn.6470941.abstract: EEElectrochemical ammonia oxidation reaction (AOR), a core step in ammonia‐energy conversion, directly affects the hydrogen-production efficiency and operational stability of ammonia fuel cells. Nevertheless, the state-of-the-art Pt catalysts suffer from agglomeration-induced deactivation under harsh electrochemical conditions. Herein, highly dispersed platinum nanoparticles stabilized on carbon nanotubes (Pt NPs/CNTS-JH) were designed and synthesize as high-performance nanocatalysts via an ultrafast Joule-heating (JH) strategy for eEElectrochemical AOR. The second-scale thermal process enables the rapid formation of small, uniformly dispersed Pt active sites without surfactants or strong reducing agents, while the CNTs confinement effect synchronously suppresses particle migration and growth, thereby significantly enhancing both AOR activity and stability. Specially, Pt NPs/CNTS-JH deliver a peak AOR current density of 10.7 mA cm-2 at 0.7 V and retain 90.15% of the initial peak after 1,000 cycles in an alkaline electrolyte. Furthermore, a rechargeable zinc–ammonia battery assembled with Pt/CNTs-JH operates stably for over 12 h at a current density of 14 mA cm-2, demonstrating excellent durability. This study introduces an innovative approach to developing efficient AOR electrocatalysts and informs materials design for high-performance ammonia energy–conversion devices.

10.2139/ssrn.6517202.abstract: This study reports on the fabrication of porous conductive Ti-Fe-Cr-Si-C/Al₂O₃ ceramic-matrix composites via self-propagating high-temperature synthesis (SHS, also known as combustion synthesis) using low-cost natural ilmenite and quartz minerals. Investigation of the reaction kinetics and phase formation revealed that silicon (Si) and carbon (C) concentrations are critical parameters for tailoring the microstructure and functional performance. We demonstrate that the incorporation of C suppresses the coalescence of the intermetallic phase during combustion, leading to structural refinement; the average particle size of the Ti-Fe-Cr-Si-(C) phase is reduced from 4.1 to 1.3 μm, promoting the formation of a dense, highly connected percolation network. This refinement results in a tunable electrical resistivity (0.15–1.3 Ω·cm) and enhanced compressive strength (up to 23.4 MPa). Furthermore, the application of chemical-furnace-assisted combustion synthesis (CFACS) that combines SHS with a specialized chemical furnace effectively mitigates thermal gradients during synthesis (reducing the central-to-peripheral temperature difference from 320 to 70 °C), thereby ensuring structural homogeneity and minimizing residual stresses. The synthesized composites exhibit high operational stability as electric heating elements at temperatures up to 800 °C. These findings provide a fundamental basis for engineering high-performance, cost-effective porous materials for Joule-heated catalytic systems and advanced heating applications.

10.2139/ssrn.6521055.abstract: Photoelectrochemical (PEC) nitrogen reduction to synthesize ammonia from water and air as an environmentally friendly and sustainable technique under ambient conditions compared with the typical Haber-Bosch process has gained extensive attention. But the limitation of catalyst type and competitive hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) cause the low yield rate and faradaic efficiency (FE) of nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR). Therefore, it is a challenging goal to find an efficient catalyst for PEC NRR. In this work, we successfully prepared BiOBr/g-C3N4(15%) from a simple hydrothermal method and BiOBr in-suit growth on g-C3N4 for the efficient PEC NRR catalyst. At -0.5 V vs RHE, the 2D/2D BiOBr/g-C3N4(15%) photocathode exhibited a high NH3 yield rate of 227.3 μmol h-1 g-1 and a high FE of 25.1% in 0.1 M Na2SO4 electrolyte, which was about three times that of pure BiOBr and g-C3N4. In addition, BiOBr/g-C3N4(15%) also displayed excellent photoelectrochemical and structure durability. Meanwhile, we also compute the NRR catalytic performance on the BiOBr/g-C3N4 according to theoretical calculation. This work provides a novel insight to modify other catalysts for the design of high-performance PEC NRR catalysts.

10.2139/ssrn.6530160.abstract: Rare-earth ceramics are promising plasma etch-resistant coatings because they form stable fluorides. However, the industry-benchmark Y2O3 is limited by high cost and supply-chain risks. Although La2O3 is a more abundant and cost-effective alternative, its application is restricted by strong hygroscopicity. Upon exposure to air, La2O3 readily reacts with H2O and CO2 to form hydroxide and carbonate species, causing volume expansion and reducing density and structural stability. This paper describes the design and realization of atomic layer deposition (ALD)-grown La2O3-Al2O3 composite ceramic films that achieve etch resistance approaching that of Y2O3 while significantly outperforming Al2O3, together with improved environmental stability. Compared with Al2O3, the enhanced etch resistance of the composite films is associated with preferential removal of Al-containing fluorides, which promotes near-surface La enrichment and the formation of a dense La-rich protective layer that suppresses further erosion. Meanwhile, the incorporation of Al2O3 improves the environmental stability of the films by lowering surface basicity, thereby suppressing adsorption of ambient H2O and CO2. Under CF4/O2/Ar plasma, the composite film with 28 at.% La reduces the etch rate of Al2O3 by over 75% to 0.51 nm/min, approaching pure La2O3 (0.33 nm/min), which outperforms the industrial-benchmark Y2O3 (0.53 nm/min).

10.2139/ssrn.6530940.abstract: The direct conversion of pollutant nitrogen oxides (NOx) into valuable ammonia (NH3) represents an ideal route toward closing the nitrogen cycle and achieving sustainable development, which remains challenging due to limited catalyst functionality. Herein, we develop a Fe3O4 nanoparticle-loaded 3D honeycomb-like carbon–nitrogen material (Fe3O4@3D HS), and construct an efficient “NO oxidation–nitrate electroreduction” cascade system. In addition, during the NO oxidation stage, a micro-nano-bubble method is adopted, which can cooperate with Fe3O4@3D HS to activate H2O2 via a Fenton-like reaction, significantly enhancing the NO-to-NO3- conversion efficiency from 15% to 83%. Interestingly, during the electrocatalytic reduction stage, the same catalyst exhibits outstanding nitrate reduction reaction (NO3--RR) performance at –0.6 V (vs. RHE), achieving a Faradaic efficiency of 91.6% and an NH3 production rate of 32 mg h-1 mgcat-1. Finally, by directly utilizing the nitrate solution produced from oxidation step for electrocatalysis, a high Faradaic efficiency of 90.3% is maintained even at 134 mM nitrate, successfully demonstrating the complete pathway from NO to NH3. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) reveal that the hierarchical micro-meso-macroporous framework, coupled with high graphitization shows a reduced work function (4.39 eV), significantly enhancing the mass transport and interfacial charge transfer. Mechanistic investigations employing in-situ differential electrochemical mass spectrometry (DEMS) and density functional theory (DFT) substantiate a "deoxygenation-first, subsequent-hydrogenation" pathway, identifying the hydrogenation of *NO to *HNO as the rate-determining step. This work not only provides a high-performance bifunctional catalyst, but also offers a new paradigm for resource-oriented treatment of nitrogen pollutants.

10.2139/ssrn.6543210.abstract: Plasma-activated water (PAW) was investigated as an oxidizing precursor in atomic layer deposition (ALD) of Al2O3 films on Si(100) in the temperature range of 100–200 °C for 250, 500, and 1000 deposition cycles. PAW was produced using a pin-to-liquid plasma system, and depositions were carried out using trimethylaluminum (TMA) with different oxidants: PAW, deionized water, aqueous solutions containing O3, H2O2, NO3−, and a composite solution combining all three species at concentrations matching those found in PAW. PAW-ALD produced thicker films than conventional ALD, demonstrating enhanced surface oxidation efficiency, particularly at low temperatures, with a growth per cycle (GPC) increase of up to 17.98% at 100 °C. While film thickness slightly increased with temperature for conventional ALD, an opposite trend was observed for PAW-ALD. Among the individual aqueous solutions, only nitrate-containing solutions led to an increase in film thickness, though not to the same extent as PAW, indicating that additional species or synergistic effects in PAW contribute to the growth enhancement. Film characterization by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), and reflectance spectroscopy confirmed near-ideal stoichiometry and optical properties comparable to conventionally deposited films, indicating that PAW enhances growth kinetics without degrading film quality. The results suggest that nitrates may contribute to surface oxidation through direct reaction with surface methyl groups or through water-cluster-mediated transport mechanisms, though the complete elucidation of PAW-ALD chemistry requires further investigation.

10.2139/ssrn.6560242.abstract: Ammonia (NH3) is emerging as a promising carbon-free energy carrier, but its practical application is hindered by the lack of efficient and cost-effective catalysts for both its synthesis and utilization. Herein, a bifunctional catalytic system based on Co3Mo3N (CMN) is developed for both direct-ammonia protonic ceramic fuel cells and protonic ceramic electrochemical ammonia synthesis. CMN exhibits strong NH3 adsorption and cracking capability, lowering the temperature required for near-complete NH3 conversion to about 550 °C. When employed as an anode catalytic layer of direct-ammonia protonic ceramic fuel cells, it enables a peak power density of 728 mW cm-2 at 650 °C and stable operation for 165 h. As a CMN-based composite cathode for electrochemical ammonia synthesis, it enhances N2 adsorption and delivers an NH3 production rate of 1.34×10-8 mol s-1 cm-2 at 550 °C and 0.4 V. Density functional theory calculations reveal that CMN facilitates N2 adsorption/activation and shifts the rate-limiting step from the energetically demanding initial hydrogenation on Ni to a later step with a lower barrier. This work demonstrates a CMN-based non-noble-metal catalytic strategy for coupling electrochemical ammonia synthesis with direct ammonia power generation, thereby enabling a closed-loop ammonia energy cycle in protonic ceramic devices.

10.2139/ssrn.6575063.abstract: Solar-driven interfacial evaporation (SDIE) is a promising sustainable technology for water purification but remains limited in treating highly contaminated electronic-waste (e-waste) leachates due to diffusion-limited adsorption, unstable interfacial transport, and solar intermittency. Here, we develop a hierarchical photothermal-adsorptive evaporator by integrating flash-Joule carbon (FJC), a dual-network hydrogel framework, and phase-change microcapsules (PCMs) to synergistically regulate energy utilization, mass transfer, and thermal stability. The ultrafast-derived FJC enables efficient broadband photothermal conversion and abundant adsorption accessibility. Under one-sun irradiation, the system achieves a high evaporation rate of 3.42 kg·m-2·h-1 and 96.7% solar-to-vapor efficiency while maintaining stable operation in strongly acidic and high-salinity environments. Persistent evaporation induces directional capillary-driven advection, accelerating heavy-metal adsorption kinetics by 1.3-1.8 times and intrinsically coupling steam generation with contaminant immobilization. This work establishes evaporation-induced advective regulation as a general strategy to overcome diffusion limitations, advancing SDIE toward active interfacial mass-transfer control for complex wastewater remediation.

10.2139/ssrn.6584782.abstract: Ammonia-mediated direct reduction of iron oxide offers a low-carbon route for preparing iron-based powders, integrating the green advantages of hydrogen reduction with the easy storage and transport of ammonia. However, compared to conventional H2 reduction, nitrogen introduction and high-temperature NH3 decomposition complicate the reaction pathways, posing challenges for controlled synthesis of target phases. Thus, the reaction pathway, nitridation mechanism, and kinetics of NH3 reduction of Fe2O3 were investigated to elucidate the formation mechanisms of ultrafine Fe3N and metallic Fe powders. With increasing temperature, the reduction proceeds sequentially from Fe3O4 (400 ℃) to intermediate Fe3N (500 ℃) and finally to Fe (≥600 ℃). Complete Fe3N formation requires ≥40% NH3 concentration and sufficient nitrogen chemical potential provided by a N2 atmosphere. Mechanistic studies reveal that Fe3N follows a direct nitridation pathway of " Fe2O3 → Fe3O4 → Fe3N", confirming the dual role of NH3 as both reductant and nitrogen source. Microstructural analysis shows that the high specific surface area and porous structure of the initial Fe2O3 facilitate complete reaction, while volume expansion during Fe3N formation leads to particle refinement and increased porosity, contributing to the ultrafine nature of the obtained powders. Kinetic analysis reveals that the reduction process is successively controlled by interfacial chemical reaction, nucleation and growth, and diffusion through the product layer, with the apparent activation energy increasing at higher NH3 concentrations. This study provides data support for developing NH3-based processes to produce ultrafine iron-based powders.

10.2139/ssrn.6630545.abstract: The expansion of the lithium-ion battery industry is accompanied by the growing challenge of large-scale battery retirement. Under the dual-carbon strategy, the efficient treatment of spent batteries has become urgent to alleviate resource supply–demand imbalances and environmental pressure. Lattice distortion and dead-lithium accumulation caused by long-term cycling severely limit the direct reuse potential of spent graphite anodes. However, mainstream regeneration technologies remain constrained by high energy consumption, lengthy purification procedures, and other process bottlenecks, resulting in limited economic viability. Here, we propose a three-step synergistic regeneration strategy involving pitch coating, flash Joule heating (FJH), and acid leaching. 10.2139/ssrn.6736737.abstract: Electromagnetic pollution arising from booming communication and radar systems demands lightweight microwave absorbers with strong attenuation, broad effective absorption bandwidth, and desirable impedance matching. During the FJH process, current focusing generates interfacial hot spots, while ultrafast heating-quenching drives in situ phase transformation and nanoscale anchoring of Fe species. This behavior constructs multiphase Fe components endowed with high-density gradient Fe-C interfacial coupling. Among all as-prepared samples, C@MFe7 delivers the optimal microwave absorption performance, achieving a minimum reflection loss of −52.25 dB and an effective absorption bandwidth of 4.62 GHz at a matching thickness of 1.68 mm. 10.2139/ssrn.6753963.abstract: Vertically aligned carbon nanotube (VACNT) arrays are promising ultra‑black materials, but growing millimeters‑thick arrays with broadband absorption remains challenging. Ferrocene pre‑deposition enables precise control of catalyst density and size, balancing array thickness and light absorption. 10.2139/ssrn.6759615.abstract: The widespread deployment of renewable energy requires scalable, distributed storage solutions capable of aligning intermittent generation with continuous demand. Green ammonia is a promising energy vector, yet its production relies on the Haber Bosch process, the epitome of industrial economies of scale. This work provides a rigorous, scale-resolved assessment of where conventional ammonia synthesis ceases to be technically and economically viable. A 2-dimensional pseudo-homogeneous packed-bed model is developed to quantify the influence of radial heat losses across production scales. The analysis reveals that the assumption of adiabatic reactor operation, ubiquitous in the literature, fails below 100 tonnes per day, where conductive heat losses become comparable to reaction enthalpy. At intermediate scales, this loss necessitates additional reactor beds, while at very small scales (1 tonne per day), conventional reactor designs fail thermally. To address this, a novel variably insulated reactor concept is introduced, enabling controlled radial heat dissipation to maintain optimal reaction trajectories. This redesign reduces reactor volume and capital cost by 35–65% relative to adiabatic assumptions at scales between 1-50 tonnes per day. In addition, a comprehensive economic evaluation of the whole ammonia production process demonstrates that economies of scale fail below 100 tonnes per day, driven primarily by compression and equipment costs. Even under favourable hydrogen pricing, plants below approximately 50 tonnes per day remain economically infeasible. This study establishes the technical and economic limits of small-scale Haber Bosch synthesis and identifies targeted reactor innovations and alternative low-pressure process routes as essential for realising distributed green ammonia production.

Nevertheless, structural instability arising from lattice hydrogen extraction during catalysis severely restricts its application. Herein, we design and demonstrate the hydrogen extraction and insertion dynamic system (Ru/HWO) achieves stable and efficient photocatalytic N2 fixation. During the reaction, the release of lattice hydrogen from HWO accelerates the nitrogen reduction reaction. Active hydrogen species generated at efficient water-dissociation sites on Ru spill over onto HWO, replenishing the lattice hydrogen and thereby establishing an efficient dynamic hydrogen cycle. Benefitting from the unique mechanism, an excellent NH3 synthesis performance of 228.5 μmol g−1 h−1 is achieved, along with the full-spectrum light utilization. This study not only confirms a new lattice-hydrogen-mediated photocatalytic N2 reduction pathway, but also paves a new way for the rational design of efficient and stable hydrogen tungsten bronze photocatalytic systems.

10.2139/ssrn.6849830.abstract: Ammonia (NH₃) is a promising hydrogen carrier, yet its efficient decomposition to COₓ-free hydrogen remains challenging, especially at low temperatures. Herein, we systematically investigate the influence of calcination atmosphere (air, Ar, and NH₃) on the structure and catalytic performance of Ru/MgO catalysts for NH₃ decomposition. Comprehensive characterizations (XRD, TEM, XPS, H₂-TPR, CO chemisorption, and NH₃-DRIFTS) reveal that the calcination atmosphere critically dictates the chemical state of Ru species, their dispersion, and the metal-support interaction. Calcination in air or Ar leads to the formation of an ultrathin, irreducible RuO₂ overlayer strongly bonded to MgO via interfacial Ru–O–Mg linkages. This RuO₂ overlayer severely suppresses NH₃ activation and N₂ desorption, resulting in poor catalytic activity (NH₃ conversion <30% at 400 °C) with high apparent activation energies (109–149 kJ·mol⁻¹). Strikingly, subsequent re-calcination of these samples in NH₃ fails to convert the RuO₂ overlayer into active metallic Ru, demonstrating its irreversible nature. In sharp contrast, direct calcination in NH₃ atmosphere enables in situ reduction of Ru precursors to well-dispersed metallic Ru⁰ clusters (average size 2.3 nm) on MgO, without forming a blocking overlayer. The resulting Ru/MgO-NH₃ catalyst delivers exceptional performance: >99% NH₃ conversion at 400 ℃, a high H₂ formation rate of 575.0 mmol·g_Ru⁻¹·min⁻¹, and outstanding stability over 100 h. Its turnover frequency (2.12 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹) far exceeds those of air/Ar-calcined counterparts, and its apparent activation energy is as low as 69.8 kJ·mol⁻¹. This work not only establishes NH₃ calcination as a facile and effective strategy to construct highly active metallic Ru⁰ sites, but also uncovers the irreversible formation of a RuO₂ overlayer under non-reductive atmospheres, offering new insights into the rational design of robust Ru-based catalysts for low-temperature ammonia decomposition.

10.2139/ssrn.6864494.abstract: AbstractHigh-viscosity oil-water emulsions pose catastrophic environmental and industrial hazards, as their rigid interfacial films and extreme stickiness severely paralyze traditional separation membranes through irreversible pore fouling. To overcome this, we developed an in-situ Joule-heating PVDF composite membrane with a hydrophilic-oleophilic heterogeneous structure via electrospinning and vacuum deposition. By incorporating PEG and a reduced graphene oxide (rGO) conductive network, the membrane exhibits rapid electrothermal responsiveness, reaching 178.8 ℃ within 15 s at 50 V. Rather than relying on passive sieving, demulsification is governed by an active physicochemical mechanism in which localized Joule heating sharply reduces heavy oil viscosity and dynamically lowers the thermodynamic wetting barrier, while the in-situ polarized PVDF matrix intensely compresses the electrical double layer (EDL) of negatively charged droplets. This thermal-electro-structural synergy fundamentally breaks the colloidal thermodynamic equilibrium, driving small dispersed droplets to rapidly collide and coalesce into large oil clusters for instantaneous separation, achieving a 98.4% demulsification efficiency. Furthermore, by actively mitigating interfacial colloidal fouling, the robust membrane sustains an outstanding cumulative flux of ~120 KL/(m2·h) over 100 hours of continuous separation, offering a highly durable paradigm for complex, high-viscosity wastewater remediation.

To improve model reliability, kinetic parameters of the Temkin-Pyzhev ammonia decomposition model were estimated using experimental data through a one-dimensional (1D) gPROMS model and implemented into ANSYS Fluent through a user defined function (UDF).The developed CFD framework was applied to sphere, 1-hole, and 7-hole catalyst geometries to investigate the effects of catalyst shape on heat transfer, flow distribution, and ammonia decomposition performance. These results indicate that, contrary to the common expectation that larger catalyst surface areas improve reactor performance, the results reveal that catalyst geometries promoting superior thermal accessibility and flow penetration can achieve substantially higher ammonia conversion under endothermic operating conditions.

Zeolite 13X was identified as the most suitable candidate and implemented in a three-step pressure swing adsorption (PSA) cycle simulated in Aspen Adsorption® V14 under representative HB effluent conditions (220 °C, 150 bar, 24 mol% NH₃).The PSA cycle reduced the recycle NH₃ concentration from 2.4 mol% to 0.033 mol%, corresponding to a ~70-fold improvement in recycle cleanup. Although the PSA cycle satisfies the benchmark in terms of recycle cleanup and nominal separation energy, product dilution remains the dominant limitation. The proposed framework identifies the sorbent targets required for sorption-enhanced HB systems to become energetically competitive, providing a generalizable methodology for process–material integration studies.

This study introduces a flash Joule heating (FJH) technology to rapidly transform the weakly magnetic Fe2O3 in RM into strongly magnetic iron concentrate, enabling efficient magnetic separation. The iron content and iron recovery rate of the iron concentrate reached the highest values of 81.35% and 83.32% respectively. This FJH-based approach provides a low-energy, low-environmental-burden pathway for recovering high-purity iron from red mud, thereby promoting a circular and low-carbon aluminum industry.

In situ spectroscopy and theoretical calculations indicate that the regulated inter-site distance optimizes adsorption configurations and promotes C–N coupling. This study provides insight into distance-dependent synergistic effects in single-atom catalysts and offers a strategy for designing efficient electrocatalysts for complex reactions.

When the mass ratio of Fe2O3 to CCT is 2:1, Fe2O3@CCT-2 exhibited the best conductivity and the strongest adsorption effect on nitrogen. The Faradaic efficiency of 53.37% and ammonia yield rate of 248.00 μg h⁻¹ mgcat⁻¹ at -0.5 V vs. RHE were achieved using Fe2O3@CCT-2 as the electrocatalyst. 19 cycles of testing were conducted without a significant decrease in current density, compared to only 5 for pure Fe2O3. 10.2139/ssrn.6964498.abstract: The conventional Haber-Bosch process for ammonia production faces significant sustainability challenges, including high CO2 emissions, substantial external energy requirements, and dependence on fossil fuel-derived hydrogen. To address these limitations, this study explores a sustainable pathway for ammonia production by valorizing glycerol waste. In this regard, a novel heat-integrated reactor concept that couples aqueous-phase glycerol reforming (APGR) with ammonia synthesis (AS) is proposed. Glycerol, a renewable waste by-product of biodiesel production, serves as the hydrogen feedstock for AS, while the heat released by the AS reaction drives the endothermic APGR reaction. A rigorous mathematical model is developed, comprising a one-dimensional pseudo-homogeneous model for the AS-side and a two-phase model for the APGR-side, and validated against experimental data from the literature. Direct thermal coupling proves impractical, as maintaining the APGR-side below 250 °C (to preserve the aqueous phase) inevitably cools the AS-side below its optimal operating range (350-550 °C), limiting nitrogen conversion to about 17%. To resolve this thermal conflict, a three-tube reactor configuration with an intermediate heat-transfer oil section is proposed, successfully decoupling the temperature profiles of both reactions, achieving 68% glycerol conversion and 33% nitrogen conversion. Sensitivity analysis revealed that pressures beyond 220 atm yield diminishing conversion gains relative to compression energy costs, while maintaining an H2O/glycerol ratio of 3 and an N2/H2 ratio above 0.42 ensures hydrogen self-sufficiency. This waste-to-ammonia approach offers a promising pathway for reducing greenhouse gas emissions, waste valorization, and energy-efficient green ammonia production, warranting further pilot-scale investigation.

10.2139/ssrn.6966067.abstract: The treatment of ammonia nitrogen in urban overflow sewage requires efficient and stable technologies. Here, we report a cobalt doping strategy to modulate the electronic structure of iron oxides, creating Janus-type asymmetric Fe-Ov-Co defect sites. The distinct d-electron configurations of Co²⁺ (d⁷) and Fe³⁺ (d⁵) induce intrinsic charge polarization, forming a local built-in electric field. Using time-resolved in situ Raman spectroscopy, we directly observed surface atomic oxygen (*O, 909 cm⁻¹) as the dominant reactive species, confirming a shift from radical to non-radical oxidation pathway. The optimized Fe-8%Co catalyst achieves approximately 90% ammonia removal and 77.3% nitrogen selectivity within 30 minutes at room temperature, with negligible metal leaching over 12 cycles. This work not only demonstrates a high-performance catalyst but also provides atomic-scale insights into asymmetric oxygen vacancy-mediated ozone activation for selective ammonia conversion.

10.2139/ssrn.6967015.abstract: Microbially induced calcium carbonate precipitation (MICP) shows promising potential for coal dust suppression, but the byproduct ammonium pollution severely restricts its practical application. Herein, Sulfitobacter sp. IGS-18 was used to further simultaneously enhance coal dust suppression efficiency and in-situ byproduct ammonia removal capacity by enhancing the activity of urease, glutamine synthetase (GS), and glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH). Enzymatic assays demonstrated that Mg²⁺ significantly enhanced the activities of the three enzymes, with maximum relative activities of 158.7% (urease), 289.9% (GS), and 194.83% (GDH). The optimal Mg/Ca molar ratio was 6.0, under which compact mineralized products consisting of Mg-doped calcite and magnesium carbonate were formed. The treated coal reached a maximum hardness of 52.8 HA, with wind erosion loss of 1.7% and rain erosion loss of 8.37%. Furthermore, Sulfitobacter sp. IGS-18 supplemented with Mg²⁺ attained 90.1% NH₄⁺-N removal efficiency and reduced NH₃ emission by 94.9% relative to conventional MICP employing Sporosarcina pasteurii. Molecular docking revealed that Mg²⁺ anchored to enzyme active sites via coordination bonds with conserved Asp and Glu residues, stabilizing enzyme conformations and promoting substrate binding. This study provides a novel bacterial resource and theoretical basis for developing eco-friendly biomineralization dust suppression technology in coal mining areas.

10.2139/ssrn.6967300.abstract: Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) enables the atomic precision to engineer metal–support interfaces, yet the influence of promoter spatial distribution on catalytic performance remains insufficiently understood. In this work, trace amounts of TiO₂ were deposited on mesoporous Al₂O₃, and the variation of precursor dose and exposure time were used to decouple Ti loading from its spatial distribution. A low-dose/high-exposure strategy led to preferential TiO₂ enrichment at the external surface as confirmed by XPS, HAADF-STEM-EDS, H₂-TPR, and WDS. Although CO chemisorption shows a decrease in total exposed cobalt surface area, the modified catalyst exhibit a significant increase in turnover frequency (TOF), CO conversion, hydrocarbon yield, and C₅₊ selectivity in Fischer-Tropsch Synthesis (FTS) application. CO-DRIFTS analysis reveals a pronounced red-shift in the CO adsorption band, indicating enhanced CO activation through electronic perturbation at the Co-TiOx interface. These findings highlight the importance of promoter spatial distribution in the design of efficient metal–oxide catalysts.

10.2139/ssrn.6983090.abstract: Al2O3–Y3Al5O12 (Al2O3–YAG) eutectic ceramic with a three-dimensionally continuous interpenetrating network structure was successfully fabricated via a rapidly heated combustion synthesis chemical furnace. The effects of combustion agent mass on the microstructural evolution and solidification behavior of Al2O3–YAG eutectic ceramics were systematically investigated. The results indicate that the combustion agent mass determines the undercooling degree, melt viscosity and solidification velocity, thereby regulating the eutectic morphology from conventional ”Chinese script” structure to uniform cellular structure. When the combustion agent mass is 180 g, the inter-lamellar spacing of Al2O3–YAG eutectic reaches 1.19 μm, and the growth rate of Al2O3–YAG eutectic is up to 70.62 μm/s. Meanwhile, the Al2O3–YAG eutectic ceramic achieves excellent comprehensive mechanical properties, with a Vickers hardness of 21.58 GPa and a fracture toughness of 3.36 MPa·m1/2. This is attributed to the ultra-fine homogeneous microstructure and multiple synergistic toughening mechanisms, including crack deflection, crack bridging and crack arrest. This work demonstrates that the combustion synthesis rapid heating method is an efficient approach to fabricate high-performance Al2O3–YAG eutectic ceramics, providing a feasible strategy for rapid preparation of fine-structured high-temperature structural ceramics.

10.2139/ssrn.6985010.abstract: Copper-based alloy nanoparticle catalysts, including Cu-Ni, Cu-Zn, Cu-Fe, and Cu-Pd systems, were synthesized and evaluated for electrochemical nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR) under ambient conditions. The alloy nanoparticles were prepared using hydrothermal and thermal decomposition methods and characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD), extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The synthesized nanoparticles exhibited spherical morphologies with particle sizes ranging from 5.6 to 33.4 nm depending on alloy composition and preparation conditions. Electrochemical NRR measurements were conducted in 0.1 mol L⁻¹ Na₂SO₄ electrolyte using an H-type electrochemical cell under continuous N₂ flow. Among the investigated catalysts, Cu₁Fe₃ exhibited enhanced catalytic performance, achieving an NH₃ yield rate of 29.13 μg mg⁻¹cat h⁻¹ with a Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 2.94% at −0.3 V. In addition, Cu₁Pd₂ achieved the highest FE of 5.23%, accompanied by an NH₃ yield rate of 24.57 μg mg⁻¹cat h⁻¹, while Cu₂Pd₁ showed the highest NH₃ production rate of 30.47 μg mg⁻¹cat h⁻¹. These performances exceeded those of the corresponding monometallic Cu, Fe, and Pd catalysts prepared in this study. Control experiments conducted under open-circuit conditions and under Ar flow produced no detectable NH₃, confirming that the observed ammonia formation originated from electrochemical nitrogen reduction rather than environmental contamination or catalyst decomposition. The enhanced NRR activity of the Cu-Fe and Cu-Pd alloy nanoparticles is attributed to alloy-induced electronic structure modulation together with increased active surface area associated with reduced nanoparticle size. These findings demonstrate that alloy engineering of Cu-based nanoparticles is an effective strategy for improving catalytic activity and selectivity toward electrochemical ammonia synthesis under ambient conditions.

10.2139/ssrn.6998341.abstract: Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction reaction (NO3RR) offers a sustainable approach for ammonia synthesis at room temperature, but its efficiency is limited by the lack of catalysts with optimized activity and selectivity. In this work, Co3O4/CuxO heterojunctions were constructed on three-dimensional (3D) porous copper foams (CF) via chemical oxidation, hydrothermal reaction and calcination. This optimized catalyst integrates a stratified nanoflower morphology, abundant oxygen vacancies, and modulated electronic structures induced by strong Co–Cu interface interactions. The electrochemical evaluations of the system indicate that Co3O4/CuxO achieves an excellent ammonia Faradaic efficiency (FE) of over 98% and a high yield of 25.89 mg h−1 cm−2 at −1.0 V (vs. relative hydrogen electrode (RHE)), while demonstrating remarkable stability over 25 h. In situ spectral analysis reveals that the addition of Co promotes the adsorption of nitrate, accelerates the conversion of key *NO2 and *NHx intermediates, and increases the proportion of free interfacial water by enhancing water dissociation kinetics, thereby providing more proton supply for ammonia formation. This study clarifies the synergistic effect of heterojunction engineering and interfacial water regulation, and provides a feasible strategy for designing high-performance NO3RR electrocatalysts.

10.2139/ssrn.7004986.abstract: Driven by the EU Renewable Energy Directive (RED III) and renewable hydrogen/RFNBO targets, ammonia (NH3) cracking is becoming an important route for producing carbon neutral hydrogen (H2). Here, a dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) plasma was coupled with a Fe1-xO thermocatalyst to enhance NH3 cracking and clarify the reaction mechanism. Plasma coupled catalytic reaction (PR-CR) and catalytic reaction (CR) systems were compared over varied volume space velocities (VSV), temperatures, and voltages. 1) At 550 °C, 1060 h⁻¹ and 12 kV, the PR-CR system achieved 94.39% NH3 conversion, exceeding that of the CR system (83.33%). Catalytic pre-cracking first reduced the breakdown voltage in the DBD zone from 11 to 6 kV; after stable discharge was established, electron-impact activation, H-radical abstraction, and excited-N2-assisted pathways were generated to crack residual NH3. 2) The energy and exergy efficiencies of the PR-CR system reached 43.2% and 6.11%, respectively, higher than those of the CR system (40.46% and 3.94%), because plasma-enhanced cracking increased H2 production per unit heating input and reduced the heat-transfer irreversibility assigned to the target product. 3) After coupling thermocatalytic surface reactions with plasma kinetics and validating the model against experiments, a low-level pathway analysis of the coupled reaction was performed. Plasma kinetic analysis showed that electron-impact reactions, N2(A3)-assisted activation, and N2(V)-H2 vibrational exchange opened parallel excited-state pathways, sustaining the NH3/NH2/H2 loop and driving NH2 toward deeper dehydrogenation. This cascade strategy supports compact H2 production, distributed NH3 energy systems, and reactor design intensified by heat and mass transfer.

10.2139/ssrn.7008909.abstract: A ammonia reactor with MFI-type zeolitic ammonia-selective membrane is simulated. The reactor configuration consists of two concentric tubes, where the catalyst is located in retentate side, and the permeate side, separated from the former by a membrane, allows the selective removal of ammonia. The proposed design avoids the use of sweep gas to prevent diluting the ammonia withdrawn from the retentate side. For this purpose, a blind flange is considered at z=0 for the permeate side. The novelty consists in considering convective and diffusive mechanisms simultaneously at the permeate side, which to the best of our knowledge has still not been dealt with in the context of membrane reactors. The diffusive flux is modelled by the Stefan-Maxwell diffusion mechanism, while the convective flux is described using Hagen–Poiseuille’s law. The membrane is modeled considering permeances obtained from literature. When the total pressure of the retentate was large enough, the system showed little difference with the permeate outlet compositions surveyed. The conversion of a membrane reactor surpassed that of the Haber-Bosch process, and the fraction of the ammonia recovered at the permeate side was around 80 % with high purity. For the system under study, the diffusion mechanism cannot be disregarded.

10.2139/ssrn.7036029.abstract: Earth-abundant materials combined with scalable fabrication methods are essential for advancing photoelectrocatalytic technologies for sustainable fuel production and water purification. In this study, we report a novel process for fabricating SnxFe2-xO3 photoelectrodes using atomic layer deposition (ALD), which provides angstrom-level thickness control, excellent scalability and conformal coating of complex 3D substrates, making it a promising technique for advanced thin film photoelectrode fabrication. Tin doping was achieved through a supercycle ALD approach. A Box-Behnken Design (BBD) based response surface methodology was employed to systematically optimize the synthesis parameters. The total number of ALD cycles, fraction of SnO2 cycles, and post-deposition annealing temperature were selected as independent variables, while photocurrent density at 1.6 V vs RHE and photocurrent onset potential in a neutral phosphate buffer electrolyte were used as response parameters. Structural, compositional and morphological properties were characterized using multiple techniques. The statistical model revealed strong correlations between synthesis parameters and photoelectrocatalytic (PEC) performance, enabling identification of optimal synthesis conditions. The optimized SnxFe2-xO3 photoelectrode exhibited enhanced PEC activity for antibiotic degradation, and the underlying degradation mechanism was elucidated.

10.2139/ssrn.7102733.abstract: The development of sustainable heterogeneous catalysts for the direct synthesis of imines from readily available alcohols and amines has attracted considerable attention owing to their importance in pharmaceutical, fine chemical, and agrochemical industries. In the present study, a Cu(CH3COO)2–HT-02 catalyst was synthesized by wet impregnation of copper(II) acetate onto a calcined Mg–Al hydrotalcite-derived mixed oxide and evaluated for the oxidative dehydrogenative coupling of aromatic alcohols with aromatic amines. The catalyst was comprehensively characterized using FT-IR, PXRD, SEM–EDX, BET surface area analysis, CO2-TPD, NH3-TPD, TGA, and ICP-OES, confirming successful incorporation of highly dispersed copper species while preserving the porous mixed oxide framework. BET analysis demonstrated a high specific surface area (149.6 m2 g−1) and mesoporous structure, providing abundant accessible catalytic sites. The catalytic performance was investigated using three representative substrate combinations containing electron-donating and electron-withdrawing substituents under aerobic or oxygen-assisted conditions. Reaction optimization identified 180°C as the optimum temperature for efficient oxidative dehydrogenation and imine formation. The catalyst exhibited excellent activity, affording substrate conversions of 92.1–96.8%, selectivity of 89.6–93.2%, and isolated yields of 87.2–91.4%. Solvent-free conditions further enhanced catalytic efficiency by improving reactant–catalyst interactions. The synergistic combination of redox-active Cu2+/Cu+ centers and Lewis basic Mg–Al oxide sites promoted efficient oxidation of aromatic alcohols followed by condensation with aromatic amines to produce the corresponding Schiff bases. The catalyst also demonstrated broad substrate compatibility, structural stability, and satisfactory recyclability after repeated reaction cycles. These findings establish Cu(CH3COO)2–HT-02 as an efficient, reusable, and environmentally benign heterogeneous catalyst for the green synthesis of aromatic imines through oxidative dehydrogenative coupling using molecular oxygen as the terminal oxidant.

Raman characterization results confirm that the Joule heating sample has higher defect density and smaller graphite domain size, and can introduce more polarization loss sites than the tube furnace sample. Prepared via rapid sintering at 1100 °C, the PDN-1100 sample exhibits an RLmin of -53.49 dB at an ultrathin thickness of 1.55 mm and an EAB of 5.25 GHz, featuring strong attenuation and a broad absorption band. Microscopic and phase analysis show that the wave absorption performance of the material is synergistically regulated by the degree of graphitization and multiphase interface, and multiple losses work together to efficiently dissipate electromagnetic waves. The radar cross section simulation proves that the far-field stealth control ability of the material is outstanding. After the superstructure optimization, the radar cross section suppression effect is 14.61 dBm2 higher than that of the ideal conductor, which has excellent stealth application value. Relying on this material to build a stealth antenna model, it can provide support for the engineering landing of equipment stealth. This study reveals the internal mechanism of Joule heating regulating the microstructure and dielectric loss of SiCN aerogels, and offers a novel strategy for designing lightweight, high-performance electromagnetic stealth materials.

10.2139/ssrn.7118380.abstract: The stable mullite structure in fly ash (FA) and the stubborn olivine structure in spent lithium iron phosphate cathode materials (SLFP) are the core challenges restricting the metal resource utilization of these two types of solid wastes. This study innovatively proposes a new method of flash Joule heating (FJH) synergistic conversion of SLFP and FA (SLFP-FJH). This strategy utilizes the high-temperature shock generated during the FJH process to induce an in-situ reaction between SLFP and FA. Among them, the Li+ and Fe2+ released by the decomposition of SLFP act as charge compensation ions, effectively balancing the negative charge gap produced by [AlO4]5- replacing [SiO4]4- in mullite, promoting the fracture of the stable Bridging Oxygen in mullite and reconstituting the highly active amorphous glass phase. The effects of material ratio, FJH treatment temperature and time, and leaching agent concentration on metal leaching were systematically investigated. Combined with XRD, FT-IR, Raman and XPS, the structural evolution mechanism and charge balance mechanism of mullite transformation to amorphous phase were revealed. Kinetic studies indicated that the leaching process of the SLFP-FJH product conformed to the Avrami model. The results show that after treatment at 1800 °C for 8 s, 99.84% of Al and 99.77% of Li can be leached, and the leaching rate of Fe reaches 77.22%. Compared with traditional pyrometallurgical or hydrometallurgical processes, this technology demonstrates significant advantages in terms of processing cost and process simplicity, providing a brand-new strategy for achieving high-value utilization of solid waste and closed-loop recovery of lithium iron resources.

10.2139/ssrn.7181494.abstract: Complex oily wastewater contains emulsified oil and dissolved organic contaminants, yet conventional membranes mainly separate phases and provide limited removal of soluble pollutants. Here, we report an NCF/PTF catalytic separation membrane that integrates a nitrogen-doped carbon felt electrothermal catalytic layer (NCF) with a superhydrophilic/underwater superoleophobic polyacrylonitrile (PAN)-based separation layer formed by surface segregation. The membrane was evaluated for surface chemistry, wettability, electrothermal response, oil-water separation, dye degradation, and the catalytic mechanism. The NCF/PTF can reject oil and achieve high oil rejection (＞98%) for oil-water mixtures and emulsions (＞96%), whereas the conductive NCF layer generates localized Joule heat under a low-voltage field to activate PMS and degrade dissolved dyes, achieving the dye removal ratio exceeding 99%. Furthermore, the NCF/PTF can maintain high-efficiency oil rejection and dye removal ratios for complex wastewater containing oil and dye, even after five consecutive cycles, solely through filtration, demonstrating its ability to enable in situ, one-step purification of complex oily wastewater. This work provides a design route for coupling interfacial separation with localized advanced oxidation, representing the future direction of complex wastewater treatment.

10.2139/ssrn.7192373.abstract: Nitrate contamination poses persistent environmental and health risks, while its conversion into ammonia provides a sustainable route for nitrogen recovery. However, nitrate electroreduction in dilute wastewater is often limited by insufficient interfacial nitrate availability, sluggish charge transfer, and poor coupling between ion enrichment and catalytic conversion. Herein, we report a conductive MOF/LDH heterointerface electrode that integrates capacitive nitrate enrichment with electrocatalytic reduction, enabling a synergistic capture-to-conversion pathway for ammonia synthesis. The electrode is constructed by in situ growth of NiFe-LDH nanosheets on iron foam, followed by assembly of a conductive MOF based on 2,3,6,7,10,11-hexahydroxytriphenylene (HHTP), forming a hierarchical M-HHTP/LDH/IF heterojunction. Benefiting from enhanced charge storage, accelerated electron transport, and improved nitrate accumulation at the heterointerface, the electrode achieves a Faradaic efficiency of 85% and an ammonia production rate of 0.49 mmol cm-2 h-1 at -1.6 V versus Ag/AgCl under neutral conditions. In situ Raman spectroscopy, electron paramagnetic resonance, and 15N isotope tracing confirm a NO3- → NO2- → NH3 pathway, while density functional theory calculations reveal strengthened nitrate adsorption and reduced reaction barriers arising from interfacial charge redistribution. This work demonstrates an effective strategy for coupling ion enrichment with electrocatalytic conversion for nitrate remediation and ammonia production.

Herein, this work reports a new type of porous carbon material, porous carbonized MOF-5, with better conductive network and ion transport channel synthesized by Joule heating technology compared with traditional carbonization process, and enriched uranium effectively as high capacitance electrodes. 10.2139/ssrn.7270860.abstract: We investigated the effects of incorporating titanium carbide, a material that is naturally stable and inactive in nitrogen reduction reactions, as a host/substrate of chromium, vanadium, and niobium nitrides. These nitrides are predicted by density functional theory to exhibit nitrogen reduction reaction activity, building on our previous studies on the surfaces of nitrides, carbides, and carbonitrides. Our density functional theory calculations demonstrate that vanadium nitride overlayer on titanium carbide significantly enhances catalytic performance and reduces the onset potential to -0.27 V from -0.51 V on pure vanadium nitride, -0.58 V on vanadium carbide, and -0.52 V on vanadium carbonitride systems. The same substrate / host for niobium nitride overlayer, on the other hand, contributes to less activity by raising the potential determining energy step. The results provide significant insight for experimentalists working on overlayered structure.

10.2139/ssrn.7299344.abstract: A direct ammonia-fuelled solid oxide fuel cell (DA–SOFC) technology is a promising zero-carbon-emission power source, benefiting from the high energy density and ease of storage of ammonia fuel. Nevertheless, nickel nitridation of Ni-based conventional anodes (i.e., Ni–YSZ) under direct ammonia exposure remains a critical challenge, leading to pronounced anode degradation and, consequently, cell performance deterioration. Applying an anode catalytic layer (ACL) to the anode surface is an effective strategy to alleviate this issue. Herein, as an enabler for direct ammonia SOFCs, Ni-doped CuFe₂O₄ spinels with varying Ni loadings-Cu(1-x)NixFe2O4 (x = 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7)-were mixed with GDC as an ionic conducting phase and employed as anode catalyst layers (referred to as CNF-x) deposited on the anode support layer. Synchrotron-based XAS spectroscopy reveals two distinct local environments within the nominally cubic Cu0.5Ni0.5Fe2O4 lattice: a tetragonally distorted sub-lattice associated with Cu²⁺ and Ni²⁺ ions, and a cubic sub-lattice defined by Fe³⁺ ions. The SOFC incorporating the CNF-0.5 ACL achieves the highest power density of 810.7 mW/cm2 at 800 °C, more than a twofold enhancement compared to the bare cell (383.9 mW/cm²). The cell with the CNF-0.5 ACL also exhibited excellent stability at 800 °C, with a minimal voltage degradation rate of 0.007 % h⁻¹. The DFT computations identified that the coupling of N* adatoms to form N2* is the potential rate-limiting step in the ammonia cracking reaction on the FeNiCu cluster and Fe(110) substrate, both present on the FeNiCu/Fe(110) model. By trapping atomic nitrogen, the catalyst layer prevents nickel nitride formation and acts as a sacrificial layer, thereby enhancing anode durability, as evidenced by the superior stability.

10.2139/ssrn.7299348.abstract: Piezocatalytic N2 reduction (NRR) offers a potential route for green and sustainable ammonia synthesis. However, it is currently constrained by weak piezoelectric response, high charge transfer resistance, and insufficient N2 adsorption and activation capability. In this work, a facile hydrothermal method was employed for introducing Fe3+ into the BaTiO3 lattice to substitute Ti4+ to obtain Fe-BTO. This aliovalent substitution not only significantly enhances the piezoelectric response of BaTiO3 but also induces an optimal concentration of oxygen vacancies through charge compensation, thereby effectively promoting N2 adsorption and activation. The synergy between these two effects lowers the NRR energy barrier and accelerates charge transfer kinetics. Consequently, the optimized Fe-BTO delivers an ammonia yield of 689.3 μmol L-1 g-1 h-1 without any sacrificial agents, which is 6.7 times that of pure BTO, and retains stable catalytic performance after six cycles. It elucidates the intrinsic mechanism by which metal ion doping enhances the piezocatalytic NRR performance of BaTiO3, providing valuable insights for the design of efficient and sustainable N2 fixation systems, and offering instructive implications for advancing the application of piezoelectric materials in sustainable energy.

10.2139/ssrn.7309601.abstract: Electrochemical nitrate reduction offers a sustainable route for nitrate remediation and ammonia recovery, yet selective nitrate-to-ammonia conversion is challenged by the different adsorption and conversion requirements of sequential intermediates. A kinetic mismatch between upstream nitrate activation and downstream intermediate hydrogenation can therefore lead to transient nitrite accumulation and compromise ammonia selectivity. Here, a binder-free Cu–Fe integrated electrode (CuFe-IC/CF) was fabricated on three-dimensional Cu foam by electrodeposition. Structural and spectroscopic characterization demonstrates spatially integrated Cu- and Fe-containing species accompanied by a substantially modified surface electronic environment. Time-resolved nitrogen-species analysis reveals continuous nitrate depletion and ammonium formation, whereas nitrite initially accumulates and subsequently declines, identifying it as a transiently accumulated intermediate rather than a persistently accumulating liquid-phase product. Density functional theory calculations using idealized Cu-containing, Fe-containing, and Cu–Fe interfacial models show favorable nitrate adsorption in Cu-containing environments and an intermediate NO* adsorption regime at the Cu–Fe interface model. The latter reduces the uphill free-energy change of the potential-determining NO* → NOH* protonation step relative to the individual models. Time-resolved electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) further indicates increased availability of hydrogen-related reactive species under cathodic polarization. Consequently, CuFe-IC/CF achieves an NH4+ Faradaic efficiency of 95.5% and an NH4+ yield rate of 0.80 mg h-1 cm-2 at -0.6 V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE), together with suppressed persistent nitrite accumulation and stable performance during repeated electrolysis. These results demonstrate that balancing nitrate activation with downstream intermediate hydrogenation provides an effective strategy for selective nitrate-to-ammonia electroreduction.

10.2139/ssrn.7309695.abstract: With accelerating industrialization, nitrate (NO3–) pollution in groundwater and surface water has intensified. Currently, nitrate concentration in groundwater of some regions has reached about 150 mg L–1, severely threatening human health and the ecological environment. Among various treatment methods, Electrochemical reduction of NO3– to NH3 (NITRR) has drawn wide attention for its high efficiency, no secondary pollution and excellent environmental compatibility. Owing to excessively strong adsorption, copper-based catalysts are prone to deactivation, while cobalt-based catalysts tend to deactivate due to poisoning caused by the easy adsorption of *NO intermediates. Here, we designed and synthesized a cobalt-copper dual-site electrode material (Co-Cu/NF). The Faradaic efficiency of Co-Cu/NF for the electrocatalytic reduction of nitrate to ammonia reaches as high as 99% at - 0.45 V vs. RHE, with an ammonia yield of up to 0.85 mg h-1 cm-2, which is significantly superior to that of Cu/NF. Further conditional experiments revealed that the cobalt-copper dual sites promote the generation of hydrogen radicals (H•), thereby enhancing the NITRR performance of Co-Cu/NF. This study opens a new pathway for developing low-cost and highly efficient NTIRR materials.

10.2139/ssrn.7330982.abstract: The growing integration of intermittent renewables such as wind and solar makes effective energy storage and utilization essential for grid stability. In current literature, little attention has been given to how electrochemical systems (electrolysers) and thermochemical and electrothermal reactors respond to fluctuating power inputs typical of renewable energy sources. Their responsive ability to efficiently convert highly volatile energy inputs over extended duration remains largely unexplored. This challenge is poised to become increasingly significant as countries accelerate the deployment of renewables, necessitating energy systems that are not only efficient but also inherently adaptable to variability. To address this, we present an integrated approach that merges a Ni/CeO2/C surface-engineered catalyst prepared by selective vapor deposition with a localized Joule heating graphene architecture. This configuration enables steam methanol reforming, a reaction that converts methanol and steam to useful syngas (hydrogen and carbon monoxide) with time constants of ~10 s, achieving near-instantaneous thermal responsiveness suitable for highly volatile renewable power inputs. Furthermore, the Ni/CeO2/C catalyst exhibits a 100-fold enhancement in steam methanol reforming activity compared with its CeO2/C counterpart, demonstrating the significant catalytical benefit of Ni addition through atomic layer deposition. Both Ni/CeO2/C and CeO2/C exhibit a temperature-dependent electrical resistance characteristic of semiconducting materials, enabling direct control of reactor temperature through electrical power input.

10.2139/ssrn.7331485.abstract: Ammonia (NH3) is produced globally at nearly 200 million tons per year, primarily for agricultural applications, with its demand expected to accelerate in the carbon-neutral era due to its emerging role as a hydrogen carrier. Currently, the conventional Haber-Bosch process dominates NH3 synthesis; however, it requires harsh operating conditions (400–500 °C and 15–25 MPa) and thus consumes approximately 2% of the global energy supply. This study aims to develop a catalyst capable of synthesizing NH3 under mild conditions (400 °C and 1–5 MPa). A mesoporous carbon black (MCB) support with high surface area (1,534 m2/g) was utilized to enhance the nanoscale dispersion of Ru, which can facilitate electron transfer from promoters to the Ru active sites. The catalytic activity of the Ru-Ba combination was significantly improved by incorporating Cs, achieving high NH3 synthesis rate of 0.87 gNH₃ gcat⁻¹ hr⁻¹ despite relatively low Ru loading (~2 wt.%). XPS analysis revealed that the Ba-Cs co-promotion induces electron-rich Ru surface, evidenced by reduction in Ru binding energy alongside an increased binding energy for both Ba and Cs species, compared to singly promoted catalysts. Furthermore, H2-TPR, H2-TPD, and CO2-TPD analyses demonstrated that the Ba-Cs co-promoter enhances the reducibility, hydrogen adsorption capacity, and surface basicity of Ru catalysts, thereby creating a more favorable surface environment for NH3 synthesis. The Ru-Ba-Cs catalysts on MCB support maintained stable performance over 100 hr of continuous operation, confirming its potential as an energy-efficient and durable low-Ru catalyst for NH3 synthesis under mild conditions.

10.2139/ssrn.7331488.abstract: Ammonia is an important chemical product and a promising carbon-free energy carrier for future energy systems. As the Haber-Bosch (H-B) process is increasingly integrated with renewable and nuclear energy sources, there is a need to reassess traditional operating pressures and reactor designs. This study develops an Aspen Plus-Python optimization framework to investigate the impact of operating pressure on ammonia synthesis performance. Four design pressures (125, 180, 240, and 292 bar) were evaluated using validated ammonia synthesis kinetics and optimized reactor inlet temperatures and bedsizes.Several design criteria, including constant conversion yield, constant reactor size, targeted percentage toward equilibrium, and reactor pressure drop effects, were examined in both open-loop and closed-loop H-B systems. Results show that optimal reactor inlet temperatures increase with pressure. Reactor sizing based on a fixed percentage toward equilibrium provides a more consistent design approach than maintaining a constant conversion yieldacross different pressures. When pressure drop is considered, low-pressure systems experience the greatest performance penalty. In contrast, intermediate pressures of 180–240 bar generally provide lower electricity consumption per tonne of ammonia while maintaining reasonable reactor bed sizes. Higher pressures improve single-pass conversion and allow higher ammonia production capacities. Overall, the results indicate that intermediate-pressure Haber-Bosch systems offer a favorable balance between energy efficiency, reactor size and production performance.

10.2139/ssrn.7350325.abstract: The development of high-performance hard carbon anode materials is the key to improving sodium storage. Two typical biomasses of peanut shell and corn straw and commercial phenolic resin were used as precursors to prepare hard carbon materials at 1200 °C by Joule rapid heating technology. The effects of precursor types on the microstructure and sodium storage properties of hard carbon were systematically investigated. At the same time, the regulation of Joule heating temperature (1100-1400 °C) on the structure of hard carbon was investigated by using phenolic resin as model precursor. The materials were characterized by SEM, TEM, XRD, BET, Raman, FTIR and electrochemical tests. The results show that HC-PR has a moderate d002 (0.367 nm), a significantly lower specific surface area (23.3 m2/g) than HC-PS and HC-CS, and a reasonable defect density (ID/IG = 1.22). The reversible specific capacity is 305.2 mAh/g at a current density of 0.05 A/g, and the initial coulombic efficiency (ICE) is 77.8%. The overall performance is significantly better than that of HC-PS (ICE ≈ 73.6%) and HC-CS (ICE ≈ 67.4%). Although HC-PS has the largest d002 (0.398 nm), the high specific surface area (24.6 m2/g) leads to the irreversible consumption of some Na+ in the formation of SEI film. Due to the small d002 (0.379 nm) and the crystal impurity peak shown by XRD, HC-CS has the lowest platform capacity and slope capacity. With the increase of Joule heating temperature from 1100 °C to 1400 °C, d002 shrinks from 0.404 nm to 0.362 nm, and the specific surface area decreases significantly. In addition, the excessive shrinkage of d002 above 1300 °C leads to the decrease of reversible capacity and ICE. It is worth noting that although the d002 of HC-PR-1300 is smaller than that of HC-PR-1100, its specific surface area drops sharply to 21.0 m2/g and the defect density is more reasonable (ID/IG = 1.14). Therefore, the sodium storage performance is better than that of HC-PR-1100, indicating that d002 is not the bigger the better. 1200 °C is the key temperature to realize the synergistic optimization of interlayer spacing, specific surface area and defect density.

10.2139/ssrn.7381115.abstract: The selective catalytic oxidation of ammonia (NH3-SCO) to nitrogen (N2) is an effective strategy for controlling NH3 slip emissions from selective catalytic reduction (SCR) systems. This study reports the synthesis of CeVO4 by microwave-assisted deposition-precipitation and the preparation of RuOx-modified CeVO4 catalysts (xRu/CeVO4, x = 0-3 wt%) via wet impregnation, along with a systematic evaluation of the influence of RuOx loading on the NH3-SCO reaction performance. The results demonstrated that the incorporation of RuOx significantly enhanced the low-temperature catalytic activity of the pristine CeVO4 catalyst. The 2Ru/CeVO4 catalyst exhibited the best overall activity, achieving complete NH3 conversion at 240 °C, whereas the pristine CeVO4 reached only 98.5% NH3 conversion even at 320 °C. Comprehensive characterization by XRD, TEM, NH3-TPD, H2-TPR, XPS, and in situ DRIFTs revealed that the improved performance originates from strong metal-support interactions (SMSI) between RuOx and the CeVO4 support. At the optimal loading, the introduction of Ru increased the surface chemisorbed oxygen (Oα) content and the number and strength of acid sites. The Ru-O-V and Ru-O-Ce interfacial architectures substantially accelerated low-temperature NH3 oxidation; however, the strong oxidizing ability of RuOx lowered the N2 selectivity of all the Ru-containing samples with respect to the pristine support and made it decrease further with temperature, which reveals an intrinsic activity-N2 selectivity trade-off. These findings provide mechanistic insight into the role of RuOx in CeVO4-based NH3-SCO catalysts and offer rational guidance for the development of high-performance NH3 abatement materials.
